entries.value: CHAPTER 2  SPERM WHALE STRANDING RESCUE
APRIL 19, 2022  08:40  EMERGENCY DESK
09:10  MUDFLAT PERIMETER
14:00  LIFE SUPPORT
AFTER 19:00  TOW PREPARATION
NIGHT  TOW OPERATION
LATE NIGHT  RADIO GAP
APRIL 20, 2022  ABOUT 05:20
DAWN  COMMAND LOG
LOG AUDIT
SPECIES AND RESCUE NOTES
A phone rings in the quiet emergency room. The blank incident card will become the shared record for a rescue lasting almost twenty hours.
About eight hundred metres off Banbianshan. A huge dark shape is caught on the shallows. It can still move its tail.
Keep away from its head and tail, and do not push or tow it. From a safe distance, is the blowhole above water? Are nets or boats nearby?
The blowhole is clear and I sometimes see it breathe. There are shallows and aquaculture nets nearby. I will send my location.
RECORD E01  A caller reports a living, possibly stranded whale. Species, size, injuries and cause remain unverified.
Choose an incident title for the dispatch log.
Seventy-ton injured sperm whale stranded
Active whale reported stranded near Banbianshan
Weight, species and injury have not been confirmed. The label stays in the audit trail and may cause later teams to mistake guesses for facts.
The title matches what the caller actually reported and leaves the field team room to verify the animal.
The location and original report go through the local emergency chain to fisheries officials, fire and police services, and specialist cetacean responders.
The first team reaches the muddy shore as the tide falls. The whale remains partly submerged and moves its tail while a crowd begins to gather.
Separate people from the rescue lane. Approach only from the side. Nobody stands near the head or tail, and nobody pushes or pulls without expert approval.
RECORD E02  Distant images confirm a large living whale at this location. They cannot diagnose internal injury or explain why it stranded.
How should the perimeter team respond to the growing crowd?
Ask the crowd to push from behind the tail
Clear the head and tail zones; keep volunteers outside
A moving whale tail can cause serious injury, and an unassessed push may worsen the animal's condition. Operations pause while the perimeter is rebuilt.
Drones and flashes stop. The rescue lane stays open, and registered volunteers guide people only from outside the cordon.
I know this mudflat. I will not touch the whale, but I can report the channels and net locations from here.
Understood. Report coordinates from a safe position and stay outside the working area.
By afternoon, most of the whale is exposed. Responders report visible abrasions and peeling skin while keeping the animal wet under expert direction.
Without seawater's support, a large whale may face overheating, dehydration, breathing difficulty and pressure on its organs. Only specialists can decide the treatment and release plan.
Cover the body with wet cloth but leave the blowhole clear. Work from the side, avoid the head and tail, and never pour water into the blowhole.
RECORD E03  Log timed visible observations and trends. Do not invent wound measurements, infection levels or internal diagnoses.
One breathing interval looks different. What goes into the shared log?
Mark deterioration and order higher water pressure
Record the observation and request expert assessment
One interval is not a diagnosis, and higher pressure could send water into the blowhole. The expert withdraws the unauthorised instruction.
Observation and interpretation remain separate. Specialists can compare the timed record while approved supplies continue.
The tide begins to return. Four cards open at once: tide trend, expert assessment, tow formation and the route offshore. Waiting is not the same as doing nothing.
Published accounts describe teams keeping the whale wet until the tide provided buoyancy, then using several boats and padded attachment points for a slow tow.
CHECKLIST  Sufficient buoyancy; expert approval; padded attachment; nets cleared; every boat on a working channel.
Which preparation should the coordinator submit for approval?
One powerful tugboat for a fast pull
Several small boats, low speed and a cleared route
Wait for water; organise boats after the tide arrives
More power is not automatically safer. Minimum vessel speed and concentrated line force may exceed what the injured whale can tolerate. The plan is rejected.
The plan accounts for the whale, crew safety, route obstacles and speed limits. Experts and the field commander retain authority over timing and method.
The tidal window arrives before the formation, route and radios are ready. The rescue continues, but the lost preparation time will narrow the night-time margin.
At night, the tide begins to support the whale. After an on-site assessment, the expert agrees to a tow and the field commander authorises the boats to move slowly offshore.
Four sources remain visible: expert instruction, line-tension trend, scout reports on depth and nets, and observations of the whale's breathing and movement.
Line tension has moved from green to yellow. The whale is leaning to one side.
Do not accelerate. Pause and check the attachment point and body position first.
What message should be relayed to the boats?
Keep accelerating to save the tidal window
Request a pause and relay the expert's instruction
The expert instruction is omitted and tension keeps rising. The tow stops while crews recheck the attachment; poor earlier preparation makes the delay worse.
The full instruction reaches the commander. Once approved, the boats slow and inspect the attachment. A safety pause is recorded as control, not failure.
Farther offshore, the radio signal breaks up. The convoy has reportedly reached deeper water, but nets still have to be cleared or avoided.
Dense nets ahead. Recommend a course change. I will repeat the coordinates.
State the observation time and coordinate reference. Rear boats must not follow an unconfirmed turn.
Sort reports as RECEIVED, NEEDS READ-BACK or SIGNAL LOST. Missing information stays blank until another boat confirms it.
A current coordinate is missing. How should the record handle it?
Fill the gap with the coordinate from ten minutes ago
Mark it unknown and obtain cross-confirmation
An old position now appears current, bringing a following boat closer to the net area. The false continuity will surface during the route audit.
The log is temporarily incomplete but honest. Relay boats restore a shared position reference without inventing data.
A complete-looking log is not always a truthful one. Every number should identify who reported it and when; some boxes should remain UNKNOWN.
Around 05:20, the boats reach the planned offshore release area. Sources disagree on the exact depth, so the record says deep water rather than inventing one final number.
Dawn turns the sea from black to blue-green. After working through the night, everyone watches the water and waits for the expert's assessment.
Stop forward movement. Observe breathing, tail movement and balance. Once the release conditions are met, the operating crew may remove the tow.
The expert recommendation, command approval and boat read-back agree. The release time is logged, and vessels remain at a safe distance.
After the tow is released, the whale pauses at the surface, moves its tail and dives under its own power. The boats observe for roughly half an hour before returning.
Choose the closing statement for the incident log.
The whale fully recovered and will survive normally
The whale moved and dived; long-term survival is unknown
The team observed independent movement after release, not complete recovery. Without a full examination or tracking, the claim cannot be supported.
The conclusion matches the evidence: the tow ended and the whale moved and dived independently. Its long-term condition remains unknown.
The rescue returned a living sperm whale to deeper water. Honest limits do not diminish that achievement; they show exactly what was accomplished and what was not learned.
Back in the command vehicle, the timeline opens from first call to release. Every entry can reveal its source, time and approving authority.
Before you finish, list everything we could not confirm. The next rescue team needs to know what is missing.
No full medical examination. No tracking tag. Stranding cause unknown. Long-term survival unknown.
AUDIT  The first title presented an estimated weight, species and injury as confirmed facts. The correction remains visible.
AUDIT  An unsafe crowd instruction interrupted operations and exposed both people and the whale to avoidable risk.
AUDIT  A single observation was turned into an unauthorised diagnosis and treatment order.
AUDIT  The single-vessel force plan ignored speed and attachment limits and had to be rejected.
AUDIT  Waiting without preparing boats, route and communications reduced the later tidal margin.
AUDIT  An expert pause instruction was omitted, forcing a longer safety stop and attachment check.
AUDIT  A stale coordinate was entered as current. The route record looked complete but was not traceable.
AUDIT  The first closing claim promised long-term recovery that the available observations cannot establish.
Corrections stay in the record instead of disappearing. Unknowns remain labelled, and the log is saved for the next team.
SPERM WHALE  Physeter macrocephalus  It is listed as a Class I nationally protected wild animal in China.
A stranded whale can face overheating, dehydration, breathing difficulty, skin injury and pressure on internal organs after losing the support of seawater.
Report stranded cetaceans to the relevant fisheries or emergency authority. Keep away, avoid crowds, and never push, pull or pour water into the blowhole without specialist direction.
CHAPTER COMPLETE  TIDE BETWEEN US
